reference_title: Eurocode 7: Geotechnical Design - Part 1: General Rules

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Establishes that Section 12 applies to embankments for small dams and for infrastructure, and that placement and compaction of fill shall follow the provisions of Section 5.
sections.body: The provisions of this Section shall apply to embankments for small dams and for infrastructure. For placement and compaction of fill the provisions in Section 5 should be applied.
key_points: Applies to embankments for small dams and for infrastructure (e.g. roads, rail)
Fill placement and compaction follow the provisions of Section 5
sections.applicability: Applies to the design of embankments built from placed and compacted fill for small dams or infrastructure.

sections.title: Limit states
sections.summary: Requires a compiled list of embankment limit states, covering loss of overall site stability, embankment slope/crest failure, internal-erosion and surface-erosion/scour failure, serviceability-affecting deformation (settlement, cracking), damage to nearby structures/utilities from settlement or creep, transition-zone deformation, climate-driven loss of traffic-area serviceability, freeze-thaw creep, base-course degradation, hydraulic-action deformation, and environmental-condition changes.
sections.body: A list shall be compiled of limit states to be checked in the design of the embankment. The following limit states should be checked: loss of overall site stability; failure in the embankment slope or crest; failure caused by internal erosion; failure caused by surface erosion or scour; deformations in the embankment leading to loss of serviceability, e.g. excessive settlements or cracks; settlements and creep displacements leading to damages or loss of serviceability in nearby structures or utilities; excessive deformations in transition zones, e.g. the access embankment of a bridge abutment; loss of serviceability of traffic areas by climatic influences such as freezing and thawing or extreme drying; creep in slopes during the freezing and thawing period; degradation of base course material due to high traffic loads; deformations caused by hydraulic actions; and changes of environmental conditions such as pollution of surface or ground-water, noise, or vibrations.
key_points: Compile a limit-state list covering loss of overall site stability and embankment slope/crest failure
Include failure by internal erosion and by surface erosion/scour
Include serviceability-affecting deformation (settlement, cracks) and damage to nearby structures/utilities from settlement/creep
Include transition-zone deformation (e.g. bridge abutment access embankment)
Include climate effects: freeze-thaw/drying loss of traffic-area serviceability, freeze-thaw creep in slopes, base-course degradation from traffic
Include hydraulic-action deformation and environmental changes (water pollution, noise, vibration)
sections.applicability: Applies when compiling the design limit-state checklist for a small dam or infrastructure embankment.

sections.title: Actions and design situations
sections.summary: Requires accounting for construction/blasting/pile-driving effects, planned nearby structures, erosion from overtopping/ice/waves/rain, and shrinkage/temperature effects when selecting design situations. Design free-water and ground-water levels must reflect the most unfavourable hydrological conditions (including drain/filter/seal failure risk, and steady seepage with rapid drawdown for shore embankments), account for stiffness differences on adjacent structures, and consider effective-stress decrease from submergence when checking settlement.
sections.body: In selecting the actions for the calculation of limit states, the list in 2.4.2(4) should be considered. When deriving the actions that embankments impose on adjacent structures or any reinforced parts of the ground, the differences in stiffnesses should be considered. Design situations shall be selected in accordance with 2.2. In addition, the following special design situations shall be taken into account, if relevant: the effects of the construction process, such as excavations close to the embankment fill and vibrations caused by blasting, pile driving, or heavy equipment; the effects of structures planned to be constructed on or close to the embankment; the erosion effects of overtopping, ice, waves, and rain on the slopes and crest; and temperature effects such as shrinkage. The design free water level on the downstream embankment slope and the design ground-water level, or their combination, shall be based on available hydrological data to give the most unfavourable conditions that could occur in the design situation considered, and the possibility of failure of drains, filters, or seals shall be considered. For shore embankments, the most unfavourable hydraulic conditions should be considered -- normally steady seepage for the highest possible ground-water level and rapid draw-down of the free water level. In deriving design distributions of pore-water pressure, account shall be taken of the possible range of anisotropy and heterogeneity of the soil. When designing the embankment with respect to settlement, the effective stress decrease in the ground, due to submergence of the dry crust or the fill, shall be taken into account.
key_points: Actions per 2.4.2(4); account for stiffness differences when deriving actions imposed on adjacent structures/reinforced ground
Design situations per 2.2, plus special situations: nearby excavation/blasting/pile-driving/heavy-equipment vibration, planned nearby structures, overtopping/ice/wave/rain erosion, shrinkage
Design water levels reflect the most unfavourable hydrological conditions; consider possible drain/filter/seal failure
Shore embankments: most unfavourable condition is normally steady seepage at highest GWT plus rapid drawdown
Design pore-pressure distributions account for possible anisotropy and heterogeneity of the soil
Settlement design accounts for effective-stress decrease from submergence of the dry crust or fill
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting actions and design situations for embankments, particularly shore or water-retaining embankments subject to rapid drawdown.

sections.title: Design and construction considerations
sections.summary: Requires embankment design to draw on experience with similar ground and fill material, address foundation-level considerations (bearing stratum, climatic protection, drainage, adjacent-structure effects, low-permeability layers), and ensure adequate subsoil bearing capacity, fill-layer drainage, appropriate fill permeability, and filter/geosynthetic use where needed. Covers staged construction on weak/compressible ground with piezometer monitoring, watertightness for differential-head embankments, ground improvement extent, weight-density testing including coarse particles, erosion protection, icing avoidance, frost penetration limits, and freeze-thaw creep in transition zones.
sections.body: Embankments shall be designed taking into account experience with embankments on similar ground and made of similar fill material. When assessing the foundation level for an embankment, the following shall be considered, when applicable: reaching an adequate bearing stratum, or applying stabilising measures where this is not practicable; providing sufficient protection against adverse climatic effects on the bearing capacity of the ground; the ground-water level with respect to the drainage of the embankment; avoiding adverse effects on adjacent structures and utilities; and reaching layers with adequately low permeability. Design of embankments should ensure that: the bearing capacity of the subsoil is satisfactory; the drainage of the various fill layers is satisfactory; the permeability of the fill material in dams is as low as required; filters or geosynthetics are specified where necessary to fulfil filter criteria; and the fill material is specified according to the criteria in 5.3.2. For embankments on ground with low strength and high compressibility, the construction process shall be specified so as to ensure that the bearing capacity is not exceeded and that excessive settlements or movements do not occur during construction (see 5.3.3(2)P). When an embankment on compressible ground is raised in layers, piezometer measurements should be specified to ensure that pore-water pressures have dissipated to acceptably low values before the next fill layer is placed. For embankments retaining water at different levels, the foundation level shall be chosen with respect to the permeability of the ground, or measures shall be taken to make the structure watertight. If ground improvement is specified, the volume of ground to be improved should be designed with sufficient areal extent to avoid harmful deformations. When determining the weight of the embankment from the weight density of fill (see 3.3.3), care should be taken to include fill particles of size 20 mm to 60 mm in the density tests, since they are often not included but can have a considerable effect on the weight density. Embankment slope surfaces exposed to erosion shall be protected; if berms are designed, a drainage facility shall be specified for the berm, and slopes should be sealed during construction and planted thereafter where appropriate. For embankments carrying traffic, icing on the pavement surface should be avoided -- the thermal capacity of a pavement on an insulation layer or lightweight fill may be high enough to avoid this. Frost penetration on the crest of an earth dam should be restricted to an appropriate level. Design of the embankment slope should consider that creep movements may occur in slopes during freezing and thawing irrespective of the slope stability under dry conditions, which is especially important in transition zones such as bridge abutments.
key_points: Design draws on experience with similar ground and fill material

Foundation-level considerations: adequate bearing stratum (or stabilising measures), climatic protection of bearing capacity, drainage GWT, avoiding effects on adjacent structures/utilities, low-permeability layers
Ensure satisfactory subsoil bearing capacity, fill-layer drainage, dam fill permeability, and filters/geosynthetics per 5.3.2 filter criteria
Weak/compressible ground: specify construction process to avoid exceeding bearing capacity or causing excessive movement during construction (5.3.3(2)P)
Staged construction on compressible ground: piezometer monitoring confirms pore-pressure dissipation before the next lift
Differential-head embankments: choose foundation level for permeability or make the structure watertight
Ground improvement extent designed with sufficient areal coverage to avoid harmful deformation
Weight-density testing must include 20-60 mm fill particles, which are often omitted but can materially affect unit weight
Protect erosion-exposed slopes (seal/plant, berm drainage); avoid pavement icing via thermal capacity/insulation/lightweight fill; limit crest frost penetration
Freeze-thaw slope creep considered irrespective of dry-condition stability, especially at transition zones (e.g. bridge abutments)
sections.applicability: Applies to the geotechnical design and construction planning of embankments, from foundation-level selection through staged construction, drainage, erosion protection, and frost considerations.

sections.title: Ultimate limit state design
sections.summary: Requires all possible failure modes to be considered per Section 11 when analysing stability of part or all of an embankment, with phase-by-phase analysis for staged construction, buoyancy consideration for lightweight fill materials (per Section 10), compatible-strain strength values for mixed fill materials, attention to spatial interaction at road/watercourse crossings, and time-dependency where improved ground is analysed. Erosion, internal-erosion, and hydraulic-pressure ULS avoidance follows the provisions of Sections 10 and 11.
sections.body: In analysing the stability of part or all of an embankment, all possible failure modes shall be considered, as stated in Section 11. Since embankments are often constructed in different phases with different load conditions, the analysis should be done phase by phase and provisions specified accordingly in the Geotechnical Design Report. Where lightweight fill materials such as expanded polystyrene, expanded clay, or foamed concrete are used, the possibility of buoyancy effects shall be considered (see Section 10). Any analysis of embankments containing different fill materials shall adopt strength values that have been determined at compatible strains in the materials. Where roads or watercourses cross an embankment, special attention should be paid to the spatial interaction of the various structural elements. When analysing the stability of improved ground, the effect of the improving process, e.g. the disturbance of soft sensitive clay, should be considered; as the effect of the improvement is time-dependent, it should not be taken into account until a steady state has been reached. To avoid ultimate limit states caused by surface erosion, internal erosion, or hydraulic pressure, the provisions in Sections 10 and 11 shall be fulfilled.
key_points: Consider all possible failure modes per Section 11 when checking stability of part or all of an embankment
Staged-construction embankments: analyse phase by phase, specifying provisions in the Geotechnical Design Report
Lightweight fill (expanded polystyrene, expanded clay, foamed concrete): consider buoyancy per Section 10
Mixed fill materials: adopt strength values determined at compatible strains
Road/watercourse crossings: pay special attention to spatial interaction of structural elements
Improved ground: consider disturbance effects (e.g. soft sensitive clay) and treat the improvement's benefit as time-dependent (not counted until steady state)
Surface erosion, internal erosion, and hydraulic-pressure ULS avoidance follow the provisions of Sections 10 and 11
sections.applicability: Applies to the ultimate limit state stability verification of embankments, including staged, lightweight-fill, mixed-material, and ground-improved cases.

sections.title: Serviceability limit state design
sections.summary: Requires demonstrating that embankment deformation will not cause an SLS in the embankment itself or in nearby structures, roads, or services, with settlement on compressible ground calculated per 6.6.1 (attending to the time-dependency of consolidation and secondary effects), accounting for ground-water-driven deformation, and using pre-loading or trial embankments where deformations are difficult to predict, especially where SLS must be prevented.
sections.body: The design shall show that the deformation of the embankment will not cause a serviceability limit state in the embankment or in structures, roads, or services sited on, in, or near the embankment. The settlement of an embankment on compressible ground should be calculated using the principles of 6.6.1, with special attention paid to the time dependency of the settlements due to both consolidation and secondary effects. The possibility of deformations due to changes in ground-water conditions should be taken into account. In cases where the deformations are difficult to predict, the methods of pre-loading or trial embankments should be considered, especially where serviceability limit states shall be prevented.
key_points: Design demonstrates embankment deformation will not cause an SLS in the embankment or in nearby structures/roads/services
Settlement on compressible ground calculated per 6.6.1, attending to time dependency of consolidation and secondary compression
Consider deformation from changes in ground-water conditions
Where deformations are hard to predict, consider pre-loading or trial embankments, especially where SLS avoidance is critical
sections.applicability: Applies to the serviceability verification of embankment settlement and deformation, particularly on compressible foundation soils.

sections.title: Supervision and monitoring
sections.summary: Requires embankment supervision and monitoring per Section 4, applied when using the observational method, where dam-like stability strongly depends on internal pore-water pressure distribution, where fill/traffic pollution records are needed, where adverse structure/utility effects require control, or where surface erosion is a considerable risk. A monitoring programme, presented in the Geotechnical Design Report, should record pore pressure, settlement, horizontal displacement, fill-strength checks, chemical analyses, erosion-protection observations, permeability checks, and frost-penetration depth.
sections.body: Supervision and monitoring of embankments shall follow the provisions in Section 4. Monitoring should be applied to embankments in one or more of the following situations: when using the observational method (see 2.7); where the stability of an embankment acting as a dam to a large degree depends on the pore-water pressure distribution in and beneath the embankment; where records of pollution effects of fill or traffic are required; where control of adverse effects on structures or utilities is required; and where surface erosion is a considerable risk. In cases where a supervision and monitoring programme is required, the designer shall present it in the Geotechnical Design Report (see 2.8), and it shall be specified that the monitoring records are to be evaluated and acted upon as necessary. A monitoring programme for an embankment should contain the following records: pore-water pressure measurements in and beneath the embankment; settlement measurements for the whole or parts of the embankment and influenced structures; measurements of horizontal displacements; checks on strength parameters of fill material during construction; chemical analyses before, during, and after construction, if pollution control is required; observations of erosion protection; checks on permeability of fill material and of foundation soil during construction; and depth of frost penetration in the crest of an embankment.
key_points: Supervision and monitoring follow Section 4; applied when using the observational method, for dam-like pore-pressure-dependent stability, pollution-record needs, adverse-effect control, or significant erosion risk
Monitoring programme presented in the Geotechnical Design Report per 2.8; records must be evaluated and acted upon
Records: pore-water pressure in/beneath the embankment; settlement of the embankment and influenced structures; horizontal displacement
Records: fill strength checks during construction; chemical analyses (pollution control); erosion-protection observations
Records: fill and foundation-soil permeability checks during construction; frost-penetration depth in the crest
sections.applicability: Applies to embankments requiring ongoing supervision and instrumented monitoring, particularly dam-like or observational-method embankments.
